Published by TroubleMaker Media Group / Midgard Media LLC Boston, Massachusetts ·  ·  · Dedication To those who carry scars no one else can see, and to everyone who fought their own way out of the dark. ·  ·  · Prologue: The Chute The flesh may be bound, but the will to survive is a fire that even a century of torment cannot extinguish. Pain was not a concept anymore. It was an environment. It was the air filling Gracie Campbell’s lungs, the hot copper coating her tongue, and the blinding electric fire searing the base of her skull. She lay face down on the cold stainless steel of an operating slab. Above her, the harsh fluorescent tubes flickered with a high-pitched, maddening hum. The room smelled of scorched flesh, harsh surgical alcohol, and the ozone stench of high-voltage cautery tools. At the nape of her neck, just beneath the occipital ridge where her dark hair had been crudely shaved away, something heavy and foreign throbbed against her cervical vertebrae. It was cold—impossibly cold—like a chip of black ice burrowed directly into her brainstem. The Box. She remembered the mocking, bandaged visage of Vengeance leaning over her hours earlier. She remembered his wet, raspy laughter as the mechanical arms pinned her down. “A special gift for Blake Campbell’s precious daughter,”  Vengeance had whispered, his breath smelling of decay behind his medical mask.  “An old friend of mine. We spent one hundred years together in the dark, he and I. Every scream. Every nerve peeled back. I couldn't let his brilliant mind go to waste... so now, little bird, you will carry him forever.” Then the drill had bitten into her skull. Now, the chamber was eerily quiet. Through the heavy, drugged haze that weighed on her limbs, Gracie realized the surgical attendants had stepped out. Perhaps they believed the triple-dose of neural paralytic would keep her subdued for hours. Perhaps they thought no human being could withstand having an alien biomechanical canister spliced into their spinal column and still retain the will to twitch a finger. They were wrong. Get up... The voice didn't come from the room. It echoed directly inside her auditory nerve—raspy, dry, terrified, and vibrating with an ancient, ragged tremor. Get up! They're coming back with the clamps! They're coming back with the fire! MOVE! Gracie gasped, her fingers scraping against the polished alloy of the table. A vicious jolt of phantom agony radiated through her nervous system. It wasn't her pain—it was an echo, a hundred years of distilled terror pouring out of the obsidian canister in her neck and flooding her sensory cortex. The entity was awake. And it was hysterical with fear. Shut up,  Gracie thought through gritted teeth, blood pooling on her lip where she bit down against the agony.  Shut... up... She dragged her right arm forward. Her muscles felt like lead soaked in battery acid. Every millimeter of movement sent blinding static across her vision. She rolled her shoulder, her hip, and tumbled off the edge of the operating slab. She hit the metal deck hard. The impact jarred her fresh incision, tearing stitches and sending warm blood trickling down between her shoulder blades. She lay there for three agonizing breaths, staring at the floor grating, fighting the urge to surrender to unconsciousness. Door... they locked the blast door...  the voice whimpered in her skull, shuddering like a trapped animal.  They're going to strip our skin again... burn the wires... burn it all... “Shut up,” Gracie hissed aloud, her voice a ragged croak. She looked up. Ten feet away, set into the bottom of the bulkhead beneath a warning placard stenciled in yellow industrial paint, was an open chute. A waste disposal hatch. A cold draft drifted up from the opening, carrying the stench of rotting food, discarded biological dressings, and machine oil. She didn't have a weapon. She couldn't stand. If a guard walked through the pneumatic door right now, she wouldn't even have the strength to raise a fist. She wasn't going to kill anyone today; she was just going to survive. Gracie dug her broken fingernails into the seam of the deck plates. Pulling with her elbows, dragging her deadened legs behind her, she clawed her way forward inch by agonizing inch. Five feet. Hurry... hurry, the needles, I hear the needles!  the passenger shrieked inside her mind, flooding her visual cortex with distorted hallucinations of bone-saws and laughing shadows. Three feet. Her vision tunneled into gray static. Her heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird. One foot. She reached the lip of the chute. It was a square shaft of slick galvanized steel angling sharply downward into the facility’s lower engineering gut. Beyond it lay the automated waste collection locks where orbital disposal scows docked. Gracie didn't hesitate. She threw her weight over the threshold and let gravity take her. She plummeted through the dark. The metal walls battered her shoulders and bruised her hips as she slid at terrifying speed down three stories of exhaust piping. Then the chute opened into empty space, and she fell. She slammed down hard into a shifting mountain of compressed scrap metal, torn plastic sheeting, and rotting organic waste. The breath exploded from her lungs in a sharp gasp. Above her, the heavy hydraulic jaws of a cargo hopper rumbled. A mechanical buzzer sounded, and a massive steel pressure door slammed shut over the disposal pit with a deafening  CLANG . Total, suffocating darkness swallowed her. Beneath her, the deck vibrated violently. Deep, heavy fusion thrusters ignited with a low, rumbling groan. The space trash truck—an uncrewed, automated orbital waste scow—disengaged its docking clamps from Vengeance’s black facility and fired its sub-light engines, hauling tons of compacted refuse out into the silent, uncaring void. Gracie curled into a ball amidst the freezing garbage, one bloody hand clutching the back of her neck where the Box throbbed in the dark. We're out...  the voice in her head whispered, trembling with shock.  We're... out... Gracie closed her eyes, and the world faded to black. ·  ·  · THREE MONTHS LATER Chapter One: The Noise in the Dark Survival out on the fringe isn't about being the strongest. It's about outlasting the ghosts that follow you into the dark. The synthetic bourbon at the Rusty Anchor tasted like refined rocket propellant and stale copper, but at four credits a glass, Gracie Campbell wasn't in the mood to complain. It had been ninety days since she had tumbled out of that automated trash scow onto the rusted scrap heaps of the Outer Rim. Ninety days of nursing septic fever in abandoned cargo containers, stealing black-market antibiotics, and learning what it felt like to share a skull with an unhinged ghost. Freeport 9 hung in the hollowed-out belly of a dead nickel-iron asteroid at the outer lip of the Orion Spur, bathed in the sickly amber glow of flickering sodium lamps and sputtering plasma conduits. The air here was recycled so many times it carried the persistent tang of sulfur, grease, and cheap tobacco. It was an outlaw sanctuary, a place where mercenaries, deserters, and drifters went when they ran out of planets to flee to. It was exactly where Gracie wanted to be. Beneath her dark trenchcoat, she kept her posture relaxed, but her senses were wired taut. Across her occipital bone, the Box hummed with a low, cold vibration that sent faint static tingling through her teeth. He's looking at us,  the raspy voice whispered in her auditory nerve.  The bartender. Look at his left cuff. A syringe. He's working for Vengeance. Shoot him. Draw both guns and shoot him between the eyes before he pumps the gas! Gracie closed her eyes for half a second, breathing through her nose.  Shut up,  she thought back.  He's eighty years old and wiping a sticky counter with a dirty rag. He doesn't know who Vengeance is, and he doesn't care who I am. You're blind!  the voice hissed, panicked and acidic.  They're everywhere! The needles never stop! “One more glass,” Gracie said aloud, her voice cool and measured as she slid an aluminum credit token across the stained wood. The old barkeep poured the murky amber liquid without looking up. “You got someone waiting on you, kid. Booth six. Shady character in a corporate cowl.” Ambush!  the voice shrieked.  Drop a grenade through the ventilation grate! Burn the whole tavern! Gracie ignored the scream, picked up her glass, and turned toward booth six. A thin man in a dust-stained gray trenchcoat sat with his hands flat on the table. “Captain Campbell,” the man said smoothly. “Just Campbell,” Gracie corrected, sliding into the opposite bench. “Or Gracie, if you’re polite. What’s the job?” “A salvage contract. In the Obsidian Nebula.” The man slid a holocron across the scarred metal. “A precursor dreadnought, adrift since the First Interstellar Accord. Five kilometers of cold, unlooted alloy. My employers want the core. You bring it back, you get half a million credits.” He's lying!  the Box yelled.  It's a death trap! Look at his pulse—he's bait! Shoot his fingers off! Gracie leaned forward, her cybernetically augmented eyes scanning the holocron's telemetry. The coordinates were genuine. The radiation signatures matched precursor void-drift. “Who else knows about this wreck?” she asked quietly. “Nobody,” the broker smiled. A lie!  the Box rasped.  Baron Vargas has the same frequency! I remember that encryption... Vengeance sold that cipher to Vargas eighty years ago! Gracie’s heart hitched. For once, beneath the hysterical paranoia, the passenger’s century of captive knowledge held a grain of terrifying truth. Before she could speak, heavy magnetic boots clomped on the metal grating behind her. “Well, well,” a rough voice boomed. “If it ain’t Blake Campbell’s runaway brat. The Black Sun Cartel pays fifty thousand just for your head, little girl.” KILL THEM!  the Box screamed, blinding her right eye with flashing crimson static.  BLOW THE REACTOR! DIE BEFORE THEY STRAP US DOWN! Gracie didn't blow anything. She ducked sideways as a heavy slug slammed into the wooden backrest where her head had rested a fraction of a second earlier. In a smooth, fluid blur honed by months of running, she drew her left plasma pistol, kicked the table into the bounty hunter’s shins, and fired a blue kinetic bolt into his sternum, sending him sprawling into the corridor. “Business is concluded,” Gracie told the terrified broker, snatching the holocron. “Tell your employers  The Starlight Drifter  accepts the contract.” Chapter Two: The Starlight Drifter A ship is more than bulkheads and fusion coils. Out here, it’s the only thin shell of metal standing between your fragile lungs and the freezing mouth of eternity. Docking Bay 44 smelled of burning hydro-carbon exhaust and scorched solder. Resting in the center of the pressurized slip was  The Starlight Drifter . It was a battered, heavily modified light blockade runner, painted in mottled void-matte black with streaks of exposed gray primer where armor plating had been welded over ancient hull punctures. It wasn't pretty. It looked like an iron fist that had survived a dozen bar fights, but its sub-light thrusters were over-bored and its hyper-drive manifold was tuned to impossible tolerances. Gracie jogged up the cargo ramp, her boots ringing against the corrugated alloy. “I heard gunfire from the concourse,” a gruff, gravelly voice echoed from beneath an open maintenance hatch in the ceiling. Kaelen Voss dropped down onto the deck, wiping blackened grease from his brow with the back of a calloused hand. His left arm—from the shoulder down—was a gleaming marvel of hydraulic titanium and carbon-fiber tendons. As he rotated his wrist, the micro-servos produced a sharp, metallic whine. THE CLAMPS!  the Box screamed violently in Gracie’s ear, sending a sickening spasm down her cervical spine.  HE HAS THE SURGICAL CLAMPS! GET AWAY FROM HIM! Gracie stumbled, slamming her shoulder against a bulkhead support to keep her balance. She squeezed her eyes shut, digging her fingers into the metal until her knuckles turned white. “Gracie?” Kael frowned, stepping toward her. “You alright? You look like you just swallowed a mouthful of spent coolant.” “Fine,” Gracie forced out, her breath ragged. She mentally shoved the hysterical passenger back into the dark corner of her mind. “Just... took the stairs too fast. Bounty hunters in the concourse. We need to burn out of here before the station enforcers lock down the umbilical.” From the cockpit corridor, a young woman with a shock of electric-blue hair and a neural jack behind her right ear slid into view on a rolling technician’s chair. Tessandra Renn held a datapad in one hand, three miniature optical recon drones hovering lazily around her shoulders like silver hornets. “I’ve already sliced the docking clamps,” Tess grinned, her fingers dancing across the holo-interface. “Plus, I charged fifty gallons of fuel coolant to the Black Sun Cartel's private ledger. They’ll be furious when they check their morning statements.” “Good girl,” Gracie breathed. A heavy, measured thud shook the deck. Emerging from the armory bay was Unit-7. Standing seven feet tall, the de-shackled combat synthetic possessed a massive industrial chassis scarred by decades of warfare, carrying an arm-mounted rotary cannon that looked capable of chewing through light starship armor. “All internal security protocols active,” Seven announced in his flat, synthetic baritone. “Probability of surviving local station traffic without incoming ordnance is currently thirty-two percent. Shall I prepare primary suppressive fire?” “Just warm up the sub-light coils, Seven,” Gracie said, taking the command chair on the bridge. She slid the broker's holocron into the nav-console. “Coordinates are locked. Obsidian Nebula. Maximum burn.” Kael strapped into the co-pilot seat, glancing sideways at Gracie. He noticed the slight tremble in her right hand as she gripped the throttle, and the faint purple bruising around the collar of her shirt where the Box pulsed beneath her skin. He didn't say a word, but his jaw tightened. He's watching us,  the passenger whispered, its tone sullen and paranoid.  He wants the Box. Everyone wants to open us up... “Spool the drives,” Gracie whispered aloud, cutting off the voice. “Take us into the dark.” Chapter Three: The Graveyard of Ships The void does not bury its dead. It leaves them suspended in the frost, waiting for the living to come and remember. The Obsidian Nebula was a nightmare of cosmic radiation and dead space. For three days,  The Starlight Drifter  crept through the dense, violet-black curtains of ionized dust. Here, standard radar was useless. Subspace telemetry bounced back as meaningless static, and even Seven’s optical targeting arrays were reduced to twenty percent resolution. Yet inside Gracie’s skull, an uncanny transformation occurred. The absolute silence of the deep void seemed to soothe the raw, bleeding trauma of the Box. For hours at a time, the hysterical screams subsided into a slow, rhythmic hum. For the first time in ninety days, Gracie could think without feeling like an ice pick was being driven into her vertebrae. “Look at the forward sensors,” Tess murmured from the sensor station, her optical drones docking into their recharge cradles. “I’m picking up localized gravity wells. Thousands of them.” Gracie zoomed the main forward viewer. A collective gasp echoed across the bridge. Emerging from the dust clouds was a vast, silent necropolis of shattered starships. Miles of twisted alloy hulls, severed command bridges, and drifting engine nacelles hung in zero-gravity suspension. Some bore the blocky, utilitarian insignia of early Terran colony fleets; others were sleek, terrifying warships from alien species whose names had been wiped from galactic history. The slaughter at the Rift,  the passenger’s voice suddenly spoke. It wasn't hysterical now. It was hollow, echoing with centuries of bone-deep grief.  I was here... before Vengeance took me. We faced the vanguard. A hundred thousand souls burned in thirty seconds... Gracie’s breath caught in her throat. “You remember this place?” she muttered. “Did you say something, Boss?” Kael asked from the engineering console. “No,” Gracie covered quickly. “Just... reading the drift telemetry. Tess, where is that energy spike?” “Two hundred kilometers dead ahead,” Tess pointed toward the heart of the graveyard. “Right inside that monster.” Floating in the center of the debris was a five-kilometer-long precursor dreadnought. Its black obsidian armor was jagged, resembling a petrified leviathan with glowing violet thermal fissures running along its dorsal spine. Despite being silent for untold centuries, faint quantum emissions pulsed from its lower engineering bays like a slow, beating heart. The Aegis,  the passenger whispered in her mind, a shudder of awe and ancient dread rippling through Gracie’s nerves.  It sleeps in the dark. Vengeance hunted it for eighty years... and could never find the keys. Don't go inside, Gracie. The dead don't want us there. Gracie stood up, strapping her plasma pistols to her thighs and checking the seals on her zero-G EVA suit. “Get your helmets on,” Gracie ordered her crew. “We’re going fishing.” Chapter Four: Cold Iron and Phantom Agony Ancient machines don't care about your wars. They only recognize the code or the blood spilled across their altars. The air inside the precursor derelict was four hundred degrees below zero and dead as a tomb. Gracie, Kael, and Unit-7 floated through the breached emergency airlock, their mag-boots clicking securely against the ribbed alloy decking. Their helmet floodlights cut through centuries of stagnant void-frost, illuminating towering vaulted bulkheads inscribed with alien geometric glyphs. Turn left at the conduit,  the Box whispered. For once, the voice was steady, guided by an operative's muscle memory that predated the Union itself.  The right corridor has automated kinetic scatter-mines. Vengeance’s scavengers lost twelve men to them when they breached a sister-ship on the rim. “Take the left corridor,” Gracie commanded, pointing her rifle barrel toward a narrow maintenance conduit. Kael checked his hand-held scanner. “My readings say the primary conduit is straight ahead through the grand hall, Boss.” “Left corridor, Kael,” Gracie insisted, her voice tight. “Trust me.” Kael gave her a long, hard look through his visor, but nodded. As they passed the open grand hall, Seven tossed a spent hydro-cartridge through the doorway. An instant later, half a dozen invisible laser tripwires flared, and the corridor was pulverized by a deafening storm of high-velocity flechettes. Kael let out a low whistle over the comm. “Remind me never to play poker with you, Campbell.” Gracie didn't answer. The Box throbbed in her skull, a painful spike of feedback that made her teeth ache.  You're welcome,  the passenger grumbled with cynical pride.  Now watch out for the altar. They reached the dreadnought’s core sanctum. Suspended in the center of a massive spherical chamber was a glowing crystalline structure the size of a ground transport. It spun along three independent gyroscopic axes, casting radiant sapphire light across the frozen bulkheads. Deep inside the crystal, quantum energy swirled like a captured miniature nebula. “Mother of god,” Kael whispered, stepping forward in zero-G, his hydraulic fingers twitching. “It’s an Aegis quantum matrix. This thing could power a battlecruiser for ten thousand years... or shield a planet from orbital bombardment.” As Kael approached the primary coupling to begin the decoupling sequence, the Box in Gracie’s neck erupted in blinding, violent resonance. A high-pitched harmonic shriek tore through Gracie's brainstem. She dropped to her knees on the metal deck, clawing at her helmet collar as agonizing phantom fire burned through every nerve in her spine. The sapphire light of the core pulsed in exact synchronization with the Box. IT BURNS!  the passenger screamed in her head, thrashing like a drowned man.  THE FREQUENCY! IT'S SCRAPING MY MIND! MAKE IT STOP! “Gracie!” Kael dropped his tools, lunging toward her. Before he could reach her, the emergency proximity klaxon in their helmets blared red. Tess’s frantic voice cut through the comms:  “Gracie! Kael! We’ve got incoming! A Black Sun heavy frigate just jumped out of the nebula! They’re locking docking clamps onto the exterior hull right above you!” Chapter Five: Uninvited Guests When a syndicate warlord comes for your prize, you don't negotiate. You reload. The airlock above them didn't open; it was vaporized. A thermal breach charge blew the heavy precursor hatch inward in a hail of molten slag. Before the smoke could clear, four flash-bang canisters tumbled through the opening, detonating in rapid succession with blinding white light and concussive shockwaves. For Gracie, the flash-bang was an express ticket back to hell. The searing light tore through her optical nerves, and the Box in her skull completely lost its sanity. A century of sensory torture flooded her mind in an overwhelming tidal wave. She wasn't in a derelict starship anymore—she was strapped to Vengeance's bloody operating table, blinding surgical lamps boring into her eyes while bone-saws screamed against metal. THEY HAVE THE SAWS!  the passenger shrieked, its voice tearing through her brain like shrapnel.  KILL YOURSELF! EAT A PLASMA BOLT BEFORE THEY TIE YOU DOWN! VENT THE ROOM! SHOOT KAEL! SHOOT EVERYONE! “Get out of my head!” Gracie screamed aloud into her helmet mic, thrashing on the deck. “Hostile syndicate forces identified,” Unit-7’s calm voice cut through the madness. The combat synthetic stepped over Gracie’s trembling body, his heavy kinetic shield deploying with an electric snap. A hail of syndicate armor-piercing slugs ricocheted off Seven’s shield, painting the dark chamber in bright sparks. Seven’s rotary cannon spun up with a terrifying whine, unleashing a punishing wall of return fire that shredded the first two syndicate shock-troopers as they dropped through the breach. “Gracie, snap out of it!” Kael’s heavy titanium hand clamped down on her shoulder, shaking her hard. “We’ve got the core decoupled! We need to move NOW!” The physical shock of Kael’s grip anchored her. Gracie gasped, fighting down the blinding hallucinations. Through sheer force of will, she pushed the passenger's screams down into the dark. “I’m up,” she wheezed, rolling to her feet. “I’m up.” Two more syndicate mercenaries dropped into the chamber, wielding high-frequency vibro-blades. Duck left,  the Box suddenly whispered, shifting from blind panic into cold, ruthless survival.  His left knee has a bad servo. Gracie reacted on pure instinct. She ducked beneath a whistling blade, swept her boot hard against the mercenary’s left knee, and felt the joint snap. As he stumbled, she fired twice point-blank into his chest plate, sending his armored corpse drifting into zero-G. “Seven, grab the core!” Gracie ordered. The massive android scooped the thousand-pound glowing quantum matrix onto his armored shoulder as if it were a bag of grain. “Retreat vector clear,” Seven reported. “Estimated time until syndicate reinforcements seal the airlock: forty seconds.” “Move!” Gracie yelled, firing suppressive bursts into the ceiling breach. “Back to  The Drifter !” Chapter Six: The Fracture Jump Hyperspace is not a highway. It is a fold in the fabric of existence, and when you tear it blindly, the universe bleeds back into you. The Starlight Drifter  shuddered violently as twin plasma torpedoes from the Black Sun frigate slammed into their rear kinetic barriers. On the bridge, consoles exploded in showers of blue sparks. The smell of burning insulation filled the cockpit. “Shields down to twelve percent!” Tess yelled over the howling warning sirens. “Their tractor beam is warming up! If they pin us, they’ll crack our hull like a walnut!” “Kael, I need the hyper-drive!” Gracie slammed the sub-light throttles forward, wrenching the control yoke to dodge a barrage of railgun slugs that chewed through their outer sensor mast. From the engineering crawlspace, Kael’s voice crackled through the intercom, strained and breathless:  “The jump coils are slagged from the nebula radiation! The only way we jump is if I hook the Aegis Core directly into the primary hyper-manifold!” “Then do it!” Gracie shouted. No!  the voice in her head screamed in terror.  The resonance! Folded space will shatter the containment! It will let the memories loose! “We jump or we die in a syndicate cage!” Gracie snarled aloud. “Kael, engage the core!” In the engine room, Kael jammed the superconducting conduit directly into the glowing blue matrix. A blinding flare of sapphire energy washed through the ship's bulkheads. The hull screamed as raw precursor quantum energy flooded the drive coils. “Punch it!” Kael roared. Gracie yanked the hyper-drive lever. Space didn't stretch; it shattered.  The Starlight Drifter  plummeted into a violent dimensional fracture, bending the laws of physics around its hull. Inside Gracie’s skull, the Box overloaded. The quantum frequency tore open the locked vaults of the passenger’s digitized mind. Gracie collapsed forward over the flight yoke, her eyes rolling back into her head as consciousness was ripped away. She was falling through a hundred years of someone else’s nightmares. She felt the cold scalpels of Vengeance carving into her flesh. She felt the sensory deprivation tanks where decades passed in total, soundless agony. She saw star systems burning, fleets of precursor drones devouring worlds, and through it all, the mocking, laughing visage of Vengeance holding a small obsidian box. And then, woven into the ghost's memories, she saw her own recent past: crawling through the blood-slick operating room, throwing herself into the garbage chute, and the freezing darkness of the space trash truck. We are the same,  the ghost whispered in the dark of her mind, its voice no longer hateful, but weeping with exhaustion.  We are both broken things... discarded in the trash... Then the light swallowed them both. Chapter Seven: The Voice in the Skull The hardest truth to confess is not that you are wounded, but that the wound has become a part of who you are. Gracie awoke to the steady, rhythmic beep of a vital-signs monitor and the smell of sterile gauze. She tried to sit up, but a sharp ache flared in her ribs. A gentle hand pressed against her shoulder, keeping her down. “Easy, Boss,” Kael’s voice was uncharacteristically quiet. Gracie blinked, clearing the haze from her eyes. She was in  The Drifter ’s tiny med-bay. Kael stood beside her, his titanium arm resting on the tray table next to an open bio-scanner displaying a holographic wireframe of her skull. Tess sat on the edge of a supply crate, her eyes wide and rimmed with red. Unit-7 stood like a silent sentinel by the door. Gracie’s heart sank as she looked at the holo-display. The obsidian canister embedded in her cervical spine was clearly visible, its neural tendrils woven deep into her brainstem. “How long?” Gracie asked, her voice dry as dust. “We’ve been out of hyperspace for six hours,” Kael replied evenly. “We dropped out near an uncharted asteroid belt. The ship is safe. The core is stable. But you weren't.” He pointed at the scan. “Care to tell me why you’ve got an illegal, military-grade black box wired into your nervous system?” Gracie stared at the ceiling, swallowing hard. The Box was quiet right now—strangely, beautifully quiet. “Vengeance,” she whispered. Kael’s eyes hardened. Even out on the fringe, the name of the sociopathic warlord who had terrorized the galaxy carried terrifying weight. “He took me at Jamestown,” Gracie said, the words spilling out like old blood. “Before Blake came. Vengeance spent a hundred years torturing an operative... broke his mind, digitized his soul, and trapped him in that box. Then he surgically grafted it into my skull as a parting gift for my father.” Tess gasped, covering her mouth. “Oh, Gracie...” “I didn't wait for Blake to rescue me,” Gracie said fiercely, turning her gaze on Kael. “The second the doctors left the room, I dragged myself across the floor and threw myself down an automated garbage chute. I fell into a space trash scow and rode it out into the void. That was three months ago. I fled to the fringe because I couldn't bear to be Blake Campbell’s broken, pity-case daughter. I couldn't be locked in a Union hospital while doctors poked at my head.” Silence hung heavy in the med-bay. Then Kael did something she never expected. He let out a low, appreciative chuckle and patted her good shoulder. “Sliding down a garbage chute right after brain surgery,” Kael shook his head with genuine admiration. “Your old man might be a legend, Gracie, but you’re ten times crazier than he ever was.” “You... you’re not kicking me off the ship?” Gracie blinked. “Kick you off?” Tess chimed in, wiping her eyes. “Who else is going to let me charge black-market fuel to syndicate cartels? We’re your crew, Gracie. We don't care what’s in your head.” “Besides,” Kael added, nodding toward the engine room. “The Aegis Core is doing something incredible. Its quantum field is emitting a sub-harmonic frequency that’s stabilizing the Box. For the first time, your passenger isn't burning out your neural pathways.” Gracie touched the back of her neck. It was true. The constant, searing headache had faded to a mild thrum. Thank you,  a faint, raspy whisper echoed in her mind. Not a scream. Not a warning. A genuine expression of gratitude from a ghost that had found peace for the first time in a century. “We’re low on coolant and ammo,” Gracie said, sitting up with renewed strength. “Where are we?” “Near New Tortuga,” Kael smiled grimly. “The armpit of the galaxy. Time to go shopping.” Chapter Eight: Port of Thieves (New Tortuga) In a station where everyone is a thief, the only honest man is the one who tells you upfront how much it costs to stab you. New Tortuga was carved out of a hollowed-out nickel asteroid, spinning lazily amidst a cluster of jagged orbital rocks. It had no government, no laws, and no questions asked. Its docking bays were lined with pirate gunboats, rusted freighters, and chop-shops billowing noxious chemical exhaust into the pressurized corridors. Neon signs in five different galactic dialects advertised illegal cyberware, forged identity chips, and illicit hyper-stims. The Starlight Drifter  slipped into an unmonitored sub-level berth. Gracie, accompanied by Kael and Tess, walked down the crowded concourse of the lower market. Her trenchcoat was buttoned tight against the damp, sulfurous chill of the station air. “We need three hundred liters of hyper-drive coolant and fresh power cells for Seven’s rotary cannon,” Kael said, scanning the market stalls. “And we don't have enough credits to buy a decent sandwich.” “I know an information broker here,” Gracie replied, leading them toward a dimly lit alley beneath a massive ventilation fan. “Name’s Jax. He used to fence salvage for my father's old contacts before the war. He owes me a favor.” Jax...  the voice in her head murmured. The passenger was alert now, its tone calculating.  I know the type. Weak chin. Shifty eyes. Men like that are cowards, Gracie. Cowards don't cross a Campbell. They fear the name. He's safe. Trust him. Gracie paused for a moment. The advice sounded reasonable. For once, the Box wasn't screaming for slaughter. You're sure?  she asked internally. Positive,  the passenger insisted.  He won't dare betray you. He'll give you the coolant for free just to get you out of his sight. Gracie pushed open the reinforced blast door to Jax’s pawn shop. Behind a heavy cage of ballistic glass sat Jax—a gaunt, rodent-featured man with cybernetic magnifying loupes fitted over his eyes. When he saw Gracie walk through the door, his hands visibly twitched, knocking over a stack of electronic components. “Gracie Campbell,” Jax breathed, forcing an oily smile that didn't reach his eyes. “My word... word on the wire was you vanished into the void.” “I need coolant, Jax. And high-capacity capacitors. Off the books.” Gracie laid a handful of salvaged precursor micro-chips on the counter. “These are worth triple the cost of the supplies.” Jax’s cybernetic loupes whirred as he examined the glowing chips. Greed flashed across his face, quickly masked by nervous deference. “Of course, of course! Anything for Captain Campbell’s daughter,” Jax bowed obsequiously. “The coolant is stored in the lower geothermal refinery. Meet my runners there in twenty minutes.
